mainEntity.name: Can a tooth that needs a root canal heal on its own?

acceptedAnswer.text: Once the pulp inside a tooth becomes infected, it cannot heal without treatment. Unlike some other tissues in the body, dental pulp has a very limited ability to repair itself once bacteria have caused significant inflammation or infection. Symptoms may occasionally seem to subside temporarily, but this can sometimes indicate that the nerve has died rather than that the infection has resolved. The underlying problem typically continues to progress, potentially affecting the surrounding bone and adjacent teeth. If you suspect you may need a root canal, arranging a dental assessment is the most reliable way to understand your options.

mainEntity.name: How long can you wait before getting a root canal?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no fixed timeframe, as the rate of progression varies between individuals and depends on factors such as the extent of decay, the type of bacteria involved, and the person's overall health. However, delaying treatment generally allows the infection to advance, which can reduce the likelihood of a successful outcome and may eventually mean the tooth cannot be saved. If your dentist has recommended root canal treatment, it's generally advisable to proceed within the timeframe they suggest. If cost or anxiety are concerns, discuss these openly with your dental team — they can often help find a manageable solution.

Root canal treatment is performed under local anaesthetic, which means the area around the tooth is numbed before the procedure begins. Most patients report that the procedure itself is no more uncomfortable than having a filling placed. Any discomfort experienced beforehand — from the infection itself — is often considerably worse than the treatment. After the procedure, some mild tenderness is normal and usually manageable with over-the-counter pain relief. Your dentist will provide specific aftercare instructions. Modern techniques and equipment have made root canal treatment a far more comfortable experience than many people expect.

mainEntity.name: What are the risks of not treating an infected tooth?

acceptedAnswer.text: An untreated tooth infection can continue to spread, potentially leading to abscess formation, significant bone loss around the tooth, and in rare but serious cases, the infection can spread to other areas of the head and neck. Chronic infection also places an ongoing burden on the immune system. Additionally, the longer an infection persists, the more limited the treatment options may become — a tooth that could have been saved with an earlier root canal may eventually require extraction. Seeking timely dental advice helps ensure the widest range of treatment possibilities remain available.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if I need a root canal or an extraction?

acceptedAnswer.text: This is a decision that can only be made following a clinical examination. Your dentist will assess the condition of the tooth, the extent of any infection, the health of the surrounding bone and gums, and whether the tooth can be reliably restored after treatment. In general, preserving a natural tooth is preferred where it is clinically appropriate and offers a reasonable long-term prognosis. However, there are situations where extraction — followed by a suitable replacement — may be the more predictable and beneficial option. Your dentist will explain the reasoning behind their recommendation so you can make an informed decision.

mainEntity.name: Can a previously root-canal-treated tooth become re-infected?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, although it is not common, a tooth that has previously undergone root canal treatment can sometimes develop a new infection. This may occur if the initial treatment did not fully resolve the infection, if the seal breaks down over time, or if new decay develops around the restoration. Symptoms of re-infection are similar to those of the initial problem — pain, swelling, or sensitivity. In some cases, retreatment (a second root canal procedure) may be possible. In others, a minor surgical procedure called an apicoectomy or extraction may be recommended. Regular dental reviews help monitor previously treated teeth.
